newsitem.title: UK: Former Soviet states struggle to dump nuclear legacy.
newsitem.headline: Former Soviet states struggle to dump nuclear legacy.

text.p: Former Soviet republics, proud of speedy dismantling of inefficient centralised economies, said on Tuesday it was taking longer than expected to shake off the legacy of Chernobyl-style nuclear reactors.

Ukraine and Lithuania, under pressure from international financial and environmental organisations to close their RBMK reactors, reiterated their commitment to safety as they came under fire at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Recnstruction and Development (EBRD).
Both countries said they intended to eventually close plants at Chernobyl in Ukraine, scene of the world's worst nuclear accident in 1986, and at Ignalina in Lithuania.
EBRD President Jacques de Larosiere stressed the nuclear safety issue in a speech on Monday, saying the first in-depth safety assessment of an RBMK type reactor had just been completed at Ignalina.

"It produced a comprehensive picture of the risks of this type of plant," he said, adding that Lithuania now faced fundamental and vital choices. There are a dozen or so RBMK reactors in the former Soviet Union.
Lithuanian Finance Minister Algirdas Semeta, who fielded several questions on Ignalina at a presentation on Tuesday, said that plant was one of the safest of these reactors.
"We will try to do our best to improve safety requirements and work with the international community on this issue."

Ukrainian Finance Minister Ihor Mityukov pointed the finger at the West for delays in closing Chernobyl, where some 200 tonnes of nuclear fuel remains trapped under a reinforced concrete cover and other reactor units continue to function.

A memorandum of understanding was reached in 1995 with the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations, calling for closure of Chernobyl by 2000 in exchange for a $2.3 billion funding package to help Ukraine with the costs.

The European Union and the EBRD have also pledged significant support, but Ukraine has disputed the findings of a group of international experts who questioned the use of funds for completion of two unfinished Ukrainian nuclear plants.

"We have all wasted dangerously precious time. Namely one year and three months," Mityukov said. "Ukraine has met its obligations. Now it is the turn of our partner parties to meet their commitments."
Lithuania's Semeta could give no precise timetable for the closure of Ignalina's two units, although he said the Baltic state could find sufficient alternative non-nuclear capacity.
"The lifetime of the second bloc is longer, until 2007," Semeta said. "We still have time to find alternatives."

He told Reuters Lithuania would like to postpone until December 31, 1999 the relicensing of Ignalina One, initially scheduled for July 1, 1998, since the safety assessment programme was delayed by 18 months.
"This will be the subject of negotiations with EBRD representatives who are coming to Lithuania soon," he said.
